verses.1: After sending forth his entire army and staying on the way for only a month, Shatrughna then quickly went forth alone and swiftly.
verses.2: The brave Shatrughna, the delight of the Raghus, having stayed for two nights on the way, then went to the sacred and excellent hermitage of Valmiki.
verses.3: Having saluted the great-souled Valmiki, the best of sages, Shatrughna then stood with folded hands and spoke these words.
verses.4: Shatrughna, having arrived there for his guru's task, requested permission to stay for the night, stating his intention to depart westward the next morning.
verses.5: Hearing Shatrughna's words, the eminent sage Valmiki smiled and welcomed the great-souled and greatly renowned prince.
verses.6: Valmiki assured Shatrughna that this hermitage was indeed like his own, belonging to the Raghu lineage, and urged him to accept the offered seat, water for feet, and respectful offering without any hesitation.
verses.7: Shatrughna, the descendant of Kakutstha, then accepted the hospitality, ate the offered fruits and roots, and achieved supreme satisfaction.
verses.8: After eating the fruits and roots, Shatrughna then asked the great sage about the origin of the sacrificial splendor he observed near the hermitage.
verses.9: Having heard his words, Valmiki spoke, saying, "O Shatrughna, listen to whose abode this place formerly was."
verses.10: Your ancestor was King Saudasa, and his son was named Virasaha, who was mighty and exceedingly righteous.
verses.11: When Saudasa was still young, he went hunting and that brave king saw two rakshasas roaming about.
verses.12: These two terrible rakshasas, in the form of tigers, were devouring many thousands of animals but remained unsatisfied, never reaching sufficiency.
verses.13: But he, having seen those two rakshasas and the forest made devoid of animals, became overcome with great anger and killed one of them with a mighty arrow.
verses.14: King Saudasa, the best among men, having struck down that one demon, looked at the killed demon, now free from distress and anger.
verses.15: Having seen Saudasa looking on, the companion of that demon felt terrible sorrow and spoke these words to Saudasa.
verses.16: The demon declared, "Because you have killed my innocent companion, O most sinful one, I will therefore give you retaliation."
verses.17: Having spoken thus, that demon indeed disappeared right there, and in due course, the king became known as Mitrasaha.
verses.18: The king also performs a great Ashwamedha sacrifice near this hermitage, and Vasishtha supervised that sacrifice.
verses.19: There was a great sacrifice that lasted for many years, which became exceedingly prosperous and splendid, rivaling even the sacrifices performed by the gods.
verses.20: Then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the demon, remembering his old enmity and disguised as Vasiṣṭha, spoke thus to the king.
verses.21: The demon, disguised as Vasiṣṭha, demanded that since the sacrifice had concluded, meat-laden food should be given to him quickly without any further deliberation.
verses.22: Having heard that speech spoken by the demon disguised as a Brahmin, the king then addressed the person skilled in preparing food.
verses.23: The king instructed the cook to quickly prepare the sacrificial food with meat, making it delicious, so that the preceptor (Vasiṣṭha) would be pleased.
verses.24: Due to the king's command, the cook was bewildered, and that demon again assumed the guise of a cook there.
verses.25: He then presented human flesh to the king, saying, "This delicious food, fit for oblation and mixed with meat, has been brought."
verses.26: O tiger among men, he (the king) offered that meal, which was prepared with meat by the demon, to Vasistha along with his wife Madayanti.
verses.27: Realizing that the meat in the vessel was human flesh, the brahmin (Vasistha), overcome by great anger, began to speak (a curse).
verses.28: "Because you desire to give me this food, O king, therefore this very food shall be yours, without a doubt," (Vasistha cursed).
verses.29: Then, enraged, King Saudasa took water in his hand and began to curse Vasistha, but his wife restrained him.
verses.30: She said, "O King, because the revered sage Vasistha is our master, you are not capable of cursing back this god-like priest."
verses.31: Then, the righteous king, releasing the water imbued with anger, power, and strength, poured it onto his own feet.
verses.32: By that water, the king's feet then became spotted, and from that time onwards, the greatly renowned King Saudasa became known as Kalmashapada, the spotted-footed king.
verses.33: That king, along with his wife, having bowed down repeatedly, then spoke again to Vasistha, who was like Brahma in his wisdom.
verses.34: Having heard that the king of kings was transformed by the Rakshasa, Vasistha again spoke to the king, who was the best among men.
verses.35: The words I have spoken while overcome by anger cannot be made in vain, but I will grant you a boon.
verses.36: The duration of the curse will be twelve years, and by my grace, O king of kings, you will not remember what has transpired.
verses.37: Thus, that king, the destroyer of enemies, having endured the curse, regained his kingdom and indeed protected his subjects.
verses.38: O Raghava, the auspicious place of sacrifice belonging to Kalmashapada, which you ask me about, is near this hermitage.
verses.39: Having heard that very terrible story of the king, he saluted the great sage and entered the hermitage. इत्यार्षे श्रीमद्रामायणे वाल्मीकीये आदिकाव्ये श्रीमदुत्तरकाण्डे पञ्चषष्टितमः सर्गः ।। 65 ।। Thus ends the sixty-fifth sarga of Uttara Kanda of the holy Ramayana the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.
